To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

male banded-wrens discriminate between renditions of the trill elements of their songs based on their performance, and that the performance of the trill is important for the assessment of male quality.

males of this songbird species respond differently to songs that vary in the performance of their trilled elements, suggesting that males may use trill rate as an indicator of the quality of rival males.

male banded (or banded wren) wren (Thyrothorus pleurosticus) receivers respond more strongly to songs that have a higher rate of trilled elements, but they also respond more strongly to trills that are closer to the performance limits of the songbird vocal system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance tradeoff is not just an artifact of the vocal apparatus but rather a fundamental constraint on vocal production.

the performance of trilled songs in birds is constrained by the tradeoff between the rate and frequency bandwidth of trills, and that this constraint may be used by both sexes as a signal in social interactions.

the performance tradeoff in trilled song elements may have important implications for the evolution of song structure in birds, and that performance may be important for the assessment of rival males.
